titre: “In the Long Run, We Are All Dead”: The Real Meaning of Keynes's Line
accroche: In 1923, Keynes writes the most misquoted sentence in the history of economics, and it was not a tribute to carefree living.
contenu_vulgarise:
“In the long run, we are all dead.” The line has circulated for a century to justify not worrying about the distant consequences of a decision: spend rather than save, borrow rather than wait, enjoy now since tomorrow, anyway, no one will answer for it. It has even become a shock argument against the Keynesian school itself, accused by its opponents of preferring a carefree short term to budgetary seriousness. The problem is that the sentence doesn't say that, and its author was aiming at exactly the opposite of what he is made to say.

## What Keynes really writes, and against whom

John Maynard Keynes publishes the sentence in 1923, in *A Tract on Monetary Reform*, an essay on postwar monetary policy. He is attacking the quantity theory of money, which holds that in the long run, an increase in the quantity of money in circulation translates proportionally into a rise in prices, once the economy has returned to its equilibrium. Keynes doesn't dispute that this is true someday. He disputes that this day is of any use: “But this long run is a misleading guide to current affairs. In the long run we are all dead. Economists set themselves too easy, too useless a task if in tempestuous seasons they can only tell us that once the storm is long past, the ocean is flat again.” The target is not the future, it is inaction: saying that a market always ends up adjusting consoles no one during a crisis that drags on.

## A misreading that dies hard

The reversal of meaning is explained by the clipping: stripped of its context, the sentence reads as an admission of carelessness; put back in its paragraph, it is a criticism of those who, refusing to act, wait for an adjustment that nothing hurries them to observe. It is even the opposite of a plea for improvidence: Keynes precisely reproaches the theory he attacks for being content with a long run that never arrives in time to matter, and for ignoring what happens in the meantime (unemployment, bankruptcy, depression) while the economy, in theory, heads toward its equilibrium. The most misquoted sentence in the history of economics is therefore not a lesson in fatalism, but one of the first arguments for an economic policy that acts in the interval rather than waiting for it to close on its own.

carte.punch: “In the long run we are all dead”: Keynes was aiming at the opposite of what he is made to say
carte.idee: In 1923, Keynes writes that “in the long run we are all dead” to criticize economists who, faced with a crisis, merely say that the market ends up adjusting. A century later, the sentence circulates cut off from its context, as a tribute to the carefree attitude it was meant to fight.

quiz.question: What is Keynes really criticizing when he writes that “in the long run we are all dead”?
choix: The idea that one can predict the economic future
Economists who are content with a market adjustment that comes too late
People who save instead of spending right away
The theory that prices always fall in the long run
quiz.explication: Keynes isn't praising carelessness: he reproaches the quantity theory of money for being content with a long run in which everything works itself out, while unemployment and crisis play out in the interval.

quiz_supplementaire.question: In which work, and in what year, does Keynes write the sentence “in the long run we are all dead”?
choix: In The General Theory, published in 1936
In A Tract on Monetary Reform, published in 1923
In Essays in Persuasion, published in 1931
In a speech given to the US Congress in 1944
quiz_supplementaire.explication: The entry places the sentence in A Tract on Monetary Reform, published in 1923, an essay on postwar monetary policy, and not in the General Theory or in a speech to Congress.

quiz_supplementaire.question: What does Keynes reproach the theory he attacks with in this sentence?
choix: Presenting the return to equilibrium as a useless consolation during a crisis that drags on
Underestimating the speed at which prices rise in wartime
Ignoring the role of central banks in setting interest rates
Neglecting the impact of foreign trade on the balance of payments
quiz_supplementaire.explication: Keynes reproaches the quantity theory for being content with a market adjustment that never arrives in time to matter, not for ignoring central banks or foreign trade.
